hardware.short_description: NASA planet-hunting telescope that discovered over 2,600 confirmed exoplanets, proving Earth-sized planets are common throughout the galaxy.
hardware.educational_description: Before Kepler, scientists had confirmed only a handful of planets outside our solar system. Kepler changed everything! It stared at over 150,000 stars simultaneously for years, watching for tiny brightness dips when a planet passes in front. The result: over 2,600 confirmed exoplanets, including planets in the 'habitable zone' where liquid water could exist. Kepler's most important finding: small, rocky planets like Earth are VERY common in our galaxy — potentially billions of them!
hardware.how_it_works: 0.95m aperture photometer with a 95-megapixel CCD array monitoring thousands of stars simultaneously. Detected the tiny (0.01%) brightness dip during a planetary transit. Four reaction wheels maintained extremely precise pointing.
hardware.why_it_is_important: Kepler transformed astronomy by proving planets — including Earth-sized rocky planets — are ubiquitous in our galaxy. The discovery of billions of potentially Earth-like planets fundamentally changed the context for the search for extraterrestrial life.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Determine the frequency of Earth-sized planets in or near habitable zones of Sun-like stars.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Retired October 30, 2018, after running out of fuel. In a stable harmless heliocentric orbit safely away from Earth.
hardware.hardware_materials: Aluminum alloy structure, 0.95m fused silica mirror, silicon carbide CCD focal plane array.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA Kepler Mission records

hardware.name: Sputnik 1
hardware.location_description: Reentered Earth's atmosphere January 4, 1958 — completely destroyed
hardware.short_description: Earth's first artificial satellite, launching the Space Age on October 4, 1957, by transmitting radio beeps from orbit.
hardware.educational_description: Sputnik 1 was the first satellite ever launched into space! On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched this polished metal ball about the size of a beach ball into orbit. The world was shocked — it could be seen in the night sky and its 'beep, beep, beep' radio signal could be heard by amateur radio operators worldwide. Sputnik's launch started the Space Race between the United States and Soviet Union. It circled Earth 1,440 times before burning up three months after launch.
hardware.how_it_works: A pressurized aluminium sphere 58 cm in diameter filled with nitrogen gas to cool its radio transmitters. Four external antennas 2.4-2.9m long. Two radio transmitters broadcasting on 20.005 MHz and 40.002 MHz. Powered by three silver-zinc batteries lasting about 21 days.
hardware.why_it_is_important: Sputnik 1 inaugurated the Space Age and changed human history. Its launch shocked Western governments, sparked massive investments in science education, led to the creation of NASA, and proved that Earth orbit could be reached.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Demonstrate ability to place a satellite in Earth orbit; study upper atmosphere density through orbital decay measurements.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Burned up completely on atmospheric reentry over the Pacific Ocean on January 4, 1958, after 1,440 orbits. Nothing remains.
hardware.hardware_materials: Polished aluminium alloy sphere, aluminium nitride insulation, silver-zinc batteries, copper antenna wires.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA NSSDCA and Soviet historical archives

hardware.name: International Space Station
hardware.location_description: Low Earth Orbit (408 km altitude, 51.6 deg inclination)
hardware.short_description: Largest human-made structure in space — a permanently crewed international research laboratory orbiting Earth every 92 minutes.
hardware.educational_description: The International Space Station is the biggest thing humans have ever built in space! It is as large as a football field, has more living space than a six-bedroom house, and orbits Earth 16 times every single day. Astronauts from 20 different countries have lived and worked aboard the ISS. Scientists use the weightless environment to conduct experiments impossible on Earth: growing crystals, testing medicines, and understanding how the human body changes in space. You can even see the ISS with the naked eye!
hardware.how_it_works: Powered by eight large solar array wings generating up to 84 kW. Oxygen is provided by water electrolysis. CO2 is scrubbed by chemical absorbers. Life support systems recycle water from urine, sweat, and exhaled moisture. Communication uses Ku-band and S-band antenna systems.
hardware.why_it_is_important: The ISS is humanity's only continuously crewed space facility, serving as a platform for research in biology, physics, astronomy, and medicine in microgravity and a test bed for Mars exploration technologies.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Conduct microgravity science, test deep space exploration technologies, perform Earth observation and astronomy.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Continuously crewed since November 2, 2000. Scheduled for controlled deorbit into the Pacific Ocean in 2030.
hardware.hardware_materials: Aluminum alloy primary structure, stainless steel docking mechanisms, multilayer insulation, silica glass solar cells.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA ISS Program records

hardware.name: Spitzer Space Telescope
hardware.location_description: Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit (now 218 million km from Earth)
hardware.short_description: NASA's infrared Great Observatory that revealed dusty stellar nurseries, distant galaxies, and the TRAPPIST-1 exoplanet system.
hardware.educational_description: Spitzer Space Telescope had a superpower: it could see through cosmic dust clouds using infrared light (heat). Dust clouds around young stars hide the birth of new planets, but Spitzer could peer right through them! One of its most exciting discoveries: confirming the TRAPPIST-1 system — seven Earth-sized planets orbiting a small star, three in the habitable zone! After running out of liquid helium coolant, Spitzer continued operating for 10 more years before being retired in 2020.
hardware.how_it_works: 85cm primary mirror. Liquid helium superfluid cooled infrared detectors to near absolute zero (-272C). Instruments: IRAC (infrared array camera), IRS (spectrograph), MIPS (multiband imaging photometer). Placed in Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit to keep Earth's heat away.
hardware.why_it_is_important: Spitzer was the first space telescope to directly detect light from exoplanets. Its 16+ year operational life made it one of NASA's most cost-effective science missions.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Study the universe in infrared — from cool star-forming regions to distant galaxies invisible to optical telescopes.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Retired January 30, 2020 after 16.5 years of science. In stable, passivated Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit, drifting away at 14 million km per year.
hardware.hardware_materials: Beryllium primary mirror, titanium structure, liquid helium cryostat, silicon arsenide detector arrays.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA Spitzer Science Center records

hardware.name: TESS Exoplanet Survey Satellite
hardware.location_description: High Earth / lunar resonant orbit (108,000 km x 375,000 km)
hardware.short_description: NASA's all-sky exoplanet hunter, searching the brightest nearby stars for transiting planets using four wide-angle cameras.
hardware.educational_description: TESS is like a cosmic planet detective! It stares at large swaths of sky using four special wide-angle cameras and watches for stars to briefly dim when a planet passes in front. Unlike Kepler (which focused on dim distant stars), TESS targets bright nearby stars — much easier to study in detail afterwards. TESS has already discovered over 7,000 exoplanet candidates and will keep working as long as fuel allows!
hardware.how_it_works: Carries four MIT-designed 100mm aperture cameras each with a 24x24 degree field of view, covering a 24x96 degree strip of sky. CCDs collect light every 2 minutes. Unique high-Earth orbit in 2:1 resonance with the Moon for stable thermal conditions.
hardware.why_it_is_important: TESS provides the nearby planet targets that observatories like JWST need for atmospheric characterization. Its all-sky survey ensures no region is left unexplored for potentially habitable worlds.
hardware.scientific_purpose: All-sky survey to identify transiting exoplanets around nearby bright stars, especially Earth-sized planets in habitable zones.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Active and operational. Has observed over 93% of the sky and produced tens of thousands of planet candidates since launch.
hardware.hardware_materials: Aluminum alloy structure, four camera assemblies with anti-reflection coated lenses, CCD focal plane arrays.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA TESS Mission records

hardware.name: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
hardware.location_description: Low Earth Orbit (550 km, 25.6 deg inclination)
hardware.short_description: NASA gamma-ray observatory monitoring the most energetic phenomena in the universe — pulsars, blazars, and gamma-ray bursts.
hardware.educational_description: Fermi sees the universe in gamma rays — the highest energy form of light, even more powerful than X-rays! Gamma rays are created by pulsars (spinning neutron stars), supermassive black hole jets, and gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe. Fermi has detected over 3,000 gamma-ray sources and spotted strange Fermi Bubbles above and below the Milky Way — massive structures nobody expected to find!
hardware.how_it_works: Carries two instruments: the LAT (Large Area Telescope) covering the entire sky every 3 hours using silicon strip detectors, and the GBM (Gamma-ray Burst Monitor) detecting transient events across the sky.
hardware.why_it_is_important: Fermi made the first detection of gravitational wave counterparts in gamma rays (neutron star merger GW170817) and discovered the Fermi Bubbles — two giant gamma-ray-emitting lobes emanating from the Milky Way's center.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Investigate gamma-ray sources including pulsars, AGN, gamma-ray bursts, and dark matter; study cosmic ray propagation.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Active and operational in low Earth orbit. Continues routine sky surveys and rapid gamma-ray burst alerts in 2026. Mission planned through at least 2028.
hardware.hardware_materials: Aluminum alloy structure, silicon strip detector array, cesium iodide calorimeter crystals, bismuth germanate scintillators.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA Fermi Mission records

hardware.name: Terra Earth Observation Satellite
hardware.location_description: Sun-synchronous Low Earth Orbit (705 km, 98.2 deg inclination)
hardware.short_description: NASA's flagship Earth-observing satellite carrying five instruments to monitor land, oceans, and atmosphere since 1999.
hardware.educational_description: Terra is NASA's planet-watching satellite! It circles Earth from pole to pole 16 times per day and always crosses the equator at the same local time (10:30 AM), helping scientists compare images from different days. Terra watches Earth's forests, glaciers, deserts, cities, and oceans. It has documented Arctic sea ice retreat, tracked massive wildfires, and measured global warming. Its MODIS sensor creates daily images of the entire Earth!
hardware.how_it_works: Carries five instruments: ASTER (thermal mapper), CERES (cloud and Earth radiance), MISR (multi-angle imaging), MODIS (moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer for land, ocean, and atmosphere), and MOPITT (atmospheric CO measurement). MODIS observes every point on Earth within 1-2 days in 36 spectral bands.
hardware.why_it_is_important: Terra has provided over 25 years of consistent global climate data — a continuous record of how Earth's surface, atmosphere, and climate are changing. Used in thousands of climate science studies.
hardware.scientific_purpose: Monitor global climate change through observations of Earth's land, oceans, atmosphere, snow and ice, and energy budget.
hardware.current_or_last_known_status: Active and operational since December 1999. Operated for over 25 years — far beyond its 6-year design life. NASA managing propellant to extend operations.
hardware.hardware_materials: Aluminum and titanium alloy structure, MODIS optical bench, carbon fiber solar panels, MOPITT gas correlation cells.
hardware.verification_status: Verified from NASA Terra Mission records
